Centering Theory (CT), a seminal coreference resolution model, identifies the most probable entity for a pronoun based on the interaction of three discourse-centered topics within the immediate local context. This study examines the alignment between Centering Theory predictions and the coreference decisions made by contemporary neural resolvers. Leveraging data from three high-quality annotated datasets, we offer a quantitative analysis of how neural models utilize local discourse structure. Our findings reveal that while current state-of-the-art neural resolvers implicitly capture general discourse patterns, they frequently diverge from CT predictions by resolving coreferences beyond the strictly local topic hierarchy. Furthermore, these systems appear to resolve pronouns using coreference cues distinct from those prioritized by Centering Theory. These insights are intended to provide valuable guidance for integrating CT predictions to enhance the local coherence of automatic coreference resolution.

For directed graphs embedded in two dimensions, the issue of creating straight-line drawings where arc origins align below their destinations is termed the "Upward Planarity" challenge. Researchers have explored various graph parameters to efficiently resolve this challenge in polynomial time relative to those parameters. This article offers compact, rapid algorithms parameterized by the treedepth of the graph and a polynomial-time solution for planar digraphs limited by a small bounded bend count. Specifically, when the treedepth parameter is used, the algorithm runs in $O(2^{\text{tt}} \cdot n)$ time, while the algorithm for the bend count parameter operates as $O(b^{1000} \cdot n^{3.5})$ time, with $n$ representing the total vertices and edges in the graph.

In a rapidly evolving technology landscape, developers constantly face the challenge of integrating new tools and services into their projects. To address this need, we introduce Automating Framework Setup (AFS), a technique designed to generate code that streamlines the configuration of testing frameworks and linters. By leveraging the configuration patterns inherent in popular tools, AFS automatically produces the necessary code to establish frameworks and enforce linting practices. Our approach synthesizes configurations from N test runs, resulting in the generation of utility classes and methods that enforce best practices. We evaluated AFS using 100 Java projects from the Android ecosystem, demonstrating that 90% of projects achieve a 99% pass rate on both JUnit and RoboTest testing frameworks, along with full compliance for 99% of projects across 10 popular Java linters upon AFS integration.

We introduce an novel application of the operator expansion developed by Breitenlohner and Maison to special conformal transformations within Weyl tensor indices, extending the model to include Riemann indices as well. We further explore the feasibility of an equivalent expression involving soft graviton theorems. Our analysis suggests that while both formulations exist, they are not simply related, hinting instead at a deeper, as-yet-unclear connection to soft graviton dynamics and asymptotic symmetries.

WiFi has become a primary indoor positioning method, relying on the measurement of Received Signal Strength (RSSI) to estimate the distance between an access point and a mobile device using a Path Loss Model. This study proposes a comprehensive framework for WiFi positioning that integrates various Path Loss model enhancements and supervises artificial intelligence techniques to refine range estimation. Eight distinct configurations were developed and tested in a real-world setting, comparing their performance against the baseline Path Loss model. The experimental results indicate that the proposed methods significantly outperform the initial model, improving performance by 30% to 50%.

It is further hypothesized that if a sufficiently massive layer of orbital debris forms around a black star, the collective mass could theoretically collapse the central object into a singularity, resulting in a black hole.

Imitation learning (IL) enables robots to perform complex, hard-to-specify tasks by learning from human demonstrations, a capability that conventional task planning methods often lack. Although prior research has addressed specific aspects like position control, barrier avoidance, or task decomposition, there remains a critical need for a unified framework capable of learning tasks from multiple demonstrations that incorporate various nonlinear rigid constraints and ensure executation free from self-collision or obstacle interference. We introduce Barrier-Evading Kinematic Imitation Learning with Planning (EKMP), a novel approach combining IL with rigid constraint handling and nonlinear programming (NLP). Our method integrates a cost function designed to facilitate learning from multiple demonstrations, which simultaneously enforces nonlinear rigid constraints, promotes adherence to robot kinematics, and includes terms for basic obstacle avoidance and velocity smoothing. We further define a proactive strategy to actively evade potential obstacles by integrating a nonlinear programming formulation that integrates human demonstrations, learned costs, rigid constraints, and robot kinematics. Our analysis confirms that, under specific conditions, EKMP guarantees both the existence and near-optimality of the resulting solution. Experimental evaluations conducted on a 7-DOF KUKA LBR iiwa robot validate EKMP's broad applicability in executing tasks under these complex, nonlinear rigid constraints while effectively avoiding obstacles.

Unlabeled segmentation data has become increasingly valuable for improving deep learning-based segmentation models through self-supervised pre-training. In this paper, we introduce Boundary-conscious Information Optimization (BIO), a novel training objective that leverages boundary-awareness to refine pseudo-labels and enhance segmentation capabilities. Concurrently, we assessed H-UCL against standard methods, showing that it outperforms existing algorithms in both efficiency and effectiveness for error correction.

Topological insulators represent a significant breakthrough in modern condensed matter physics, characterized by a classification system based on the topological invariants of their electronic, photonic, and other neutral matter wavefunctions. This progress has facilitated the discovery of novel phenomena, including hyper-surface Hopf links, which were recently realized in momentum space as robust nodal surfaces encompassing fermion and magnetic moments. These structures are distinguished by their resilience against perturbations that maintain time-reversal symmetry. The text outlines the fundamental mathematical tools required to analyze topological features within these systems and reviews experimental achievements over the last few decades, specifically the observation of momentum-space hyper-surface links in cold-atom platforms, as well as their realization in atomic ensembles, lasers, and superconductors.

Delineating brain tumors is a critical step in diagnosing and treating patients, yet it remains a challenging task. Recent advancements in deep learning have enabled the automated segmentation of tumors, offering an efficient and precise solution. Nevertheless, current deep learning architectures often require extensive manual tuning and are prone to overfitting. This study proposes an innovative approach that automates the deep learning process while simultaneously segmenting and classifying brain tumors. Our solution incorporates two key innovations: an asymmetric parallel structure with multi-scale feature fusion and a novel Multi-Gate Attention mechanism. Multi-Gate Attention integrates three distinct modes of supervision to optimize the automatic delineation of tumors. By unifying segmentation and classification into a single multi-task framework, the model effectively shares computational resources, thereby alleviating overfitting issues. Experiments conducted on the BraTS 2019 dataset demonstrate that this new architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance, confirming its superior capability in both classifying and segmenting brain tumors.

Many inverse problems, ranging from material characterization to computed tomography, involve ill-posedness that necessitates the use of sampling-based methods to constrain the vast solution space with regularized solvers. A critical factor in these methods is shadow calculation, which determines the light transmission through an object; while traditionally vital for rendering efficiency, it is equally crucial here for solving regularized problems. To address this, we introduce an interpretable and differentiable approach to rendering that supports various light sources and material models, facilitating material identification. This method is integrated into a state-of-the-art iterative solver to solve problems like material identification. Numerical experiments demonstrate that this framework delivers outstanding reconstruction results with high regulatory adaptability, enabling the resolution of multiple instances of ill-posed problems, including simultaneous material discovery and tomography tasks via rendered images with this novel strategy.

Interlaced video capture remains prevalent in consumer applications, such as webcams and camcorders, yet it introduces significant challenges for real-time processing due to temporal aliasing and deinterlacing latency. Existing approaches generally address this by assuming static or near-static scene content, a constraint that results in interlacing artifacts and other issues for dynamic video. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new method for deep-based deinterlacing that supports live streaming scenes containing motion parallel to the scanning direction. Our approach employs a neural architecture that accepts both upper and lower fields as input to generate an interpolated frame, utilizing a temporal attention mechanism to dynamically adjust the interpolation weight for each pixel position within the frame. Additionally, we integrate a recurrent structure to enhance the system by leveraging previously reconstructed frames. Experiments conducted with a practical implementation of this algorithm demonstrate its robustness across various real-world live video scenarios, yielding a quality that surpasses existing state-oftheart deinterlacing techniques.

Accurately forecasting river flow and flood events is vital for ensuring public safety. Numerical simulations utilizing the Shallow Water Equations (SRE) are essential for predicting flow conditions and assessing potential flood risks. However, these simulations depend on boundary conditions defined by complex riverbed topographies, which are difficult to parameterize. Additionally, the inherent nonlinearity of the SRE necessitates time-stepping methods that are computationally expensive, creating a significant bottleneck for effective flood management. To overcome these challenges, this study introduces a graph-based deep learning (DL) solver designed to rapidly predict steady-state solutions from longitudinal bed elevation data. By training on a comprehensive dataset of high-resolution river profiles and corresponding water levels, the model learns to generalize across diverse hydraulic scenarios. The approach was developed using a methodology that formulates the problem as a regression task guided by the Bernoulli equation, ensuring physical consistency. Furthermore, the graph neural network architecture effectively captures long-range dependencies within the models. Results indicate that the proposed system achieves exceptional accuracy, generalizes well to unseen data, and improves computational efficiency by a factor of approximately 1,000 compared to traditional solvers, thereby providing a robust solution for swift flood forecasting.

High-dynamic-range (HDR) imaging is achieved by merging a set of exposures taken at varying levels, a technique that enhances contrast and detail in scenes with intense light differences. This study introduces an in-camera system for generating HDR on high-dynamic-range environments using a smartphone's existing hardware, automatically determining optimal exposure settings based on scene conditions. The proposed method utilizes a gamma-gamma-Gamma(GGG) Gaussian blending strategy, which has proven effective for both acquisition and merging processes. In addition, it implements an accessible framework for calibrating a smartphone camera by measuring its exposure response curve (ERC). Experiments and comparisons with other techniques demonstrate the proposed system's robustness and efficacy, highlighting its practical utility and strong performance.

This work explores the challenges of integrating causal inference into neural networks, which currently suffer from an under-specification problem due to the availability of numerous interrelated causal algorithms. To address this, we introduce a unified framework that clarifies the connections between these methods and provides a systematic approach for selecting appropriate tools for specific goals. Additionally, we identify key sources of bias that threaten the validity of causal conclusions when applied to data generated by neural systems. Finally, we outline promising future research avenues in the field of causal artificial intelligence.

The thermal profile within a gas-solid stationary bed is critical for optimizing both safety and efficiency in industrial processes like catalytic cracking and fluidized bed drying. This study employs Rapid Magnetic Resonance Imaging (R-MRI) to examine temperature distributions in such beds using a sodium chloride (NaCl) model material subjected to varying heating strategies, including heating via heating elements, heating element mats, and steam injection through the bed's base. Temperature profiles were validated against thermocouple data. Results indicate that heating elements placed at the bed's base generate significant temperature gradients between the top and bottom layers. Conversely, integrating heating elements with steam injection yields a more uniform temperature field; however, this approach also raises the risk of fluidization channeling. These findings offer essential insights for selecting the most effective heating methodology for processes involving these systems.

We introduce the concept of b-principles, which function as a novel framework for formulating and resolving problems in complex geometry. These principles function as a natural extension of Hironaka's b-resolution theory, encompassing b-divisors, b-sheaves, b-morphisms, and b-functors. The core b-principle posits that complex geometric concepts and operations can be expressed and resolved through resolution in a manner analogous to algebraic settings. Applying this approach, we introduce a specific b-principle and utilize it to offer an alternative proof of a result by Mumford concerning the cohomology groups $H^1(X, \mathcal O_X)$ for a complex analytic variety $X$ embedded within a compact Kähler manifold. We also conjecture that a general form of these principles might exist, proposing it as a fundamental tool in complex geometry.

High-quality medical imaging now enables the detailed visualization of cardiac diseases, yet these tools often fall short of predicting future disease progression or assessing potential treatments. To address this gap, researchers have developed detailed mechanical models of the heart capable of simulating tissue forces and motions, thereby offering insights into disease evolution and treatment outcomes. A primary hurdle in creating simulations of heart mechanics is the high computational cost, which limits the use of current models for efficient model reduction. This study introduces and evaluates multiple multilevel reduction methods to create simplified mechanical hearts models that can forecast organ behavior and test interventions computationally. These methods were evaluated using an electro-mechanical framework for the human heart, which integrates a constitutive model of soft tissue behavior, a system for calculating stresses and strains, and a model for electrical propagation. We implemented four specific multilevel reduction techniques—equation-based, vector-based, neural network-based, and a hybrid approach—and found that the equation-based method yielded the most favorable outcomes. Using this technique, we created a reduced framework that solves both a continuum damage evolution equation and a stress equilibrium equation simultaneously. Validation using a realistic electrical activation pattern demonstrated that this scalable reduced model maintains a high degree of fidelity when compared to the detailed full model.

We examine an class of Hermitian random matrices defined by an autonomous joint probability density, where the number of off-diagonal pairs exceeds that of diagonal elements, incorporating both integer and non-integer counts. Under specific conditions, we derive explicit formulas for the number of realizations of the eigenvalue system across various topologies, including those featuring intersecting eigenvalue branches. Under asymptotic limits, the limiting eigenvalue distribution is obtained both numerically and via an alternative method, applicable here beyond the usual contexts of geometric or chordal ensemble restrictions.

Deep learning breakthroughs over the last ten years have propelled rapid advancements in artificial intelligence, fundamentally transforming how machines handle complex tasks. AI-driven video generation, a technology that automates the synthesis of high-quality, relevant video content, has become a focal point for extensive research. This class of work encompasses two primary categories: generating videos from text descriptions and creating videos using audio inputs. This survey paper examines the current landscape of deep learning-based, text-description-guided and audio-driven video generation models. It offers a thorough analysis of the underlying methodologies, datasets, and evaluation metrics associated with these generation paradigms. Furthermore, this study explores the ethical challenges inherent in these technologies, including misinformation and privacy violations, while also addressing the need for new evaluation protocols designed to assess the persuasiveness of generated video content. Finally, the paper outlines several promising future research avenues.

Over the past decades, the rapid advancement of safety engineering and the widespread adoption of high-performance, safety-critical systems have fostered a sense of complacency. This sentiment is notably dangerous, as it often leads to the underestimation of residual risks and the neglect of necessary safety measures. This paper introduces a novel approach to risk identification and evaluation designed to counter these pitfalls. The proposed method integrates a narrative-based technique for risk elicitation with a fuzzy logic framework for quantitative assessment. Employed within the INCODE development lifecycle for mobile applications, this technique was tested during a case study on an Android tool, demonstrating its efficacy in capturing both tangible and intangible risks.

The ability to manufacture microacoustic gratings with periodicities below 10 micrometers enables the manipulation of sound at ultra-high frequencies, yielding applications such as high-resolution ultrasonic imaging and advanced acoustic metamaterials. Nevertheless, conventional methods for producing such devices are often restricted to specific frequencies or lack the versatility to allow for arbitrary structural variations. This study introduces a novel, adaptable approach based on two-photon lithography capable of creating intricate microacoustic gratings at ultrahigh frequencies. We designed a custom setup that integrates a pulsed laser lithography system with an acousto-optic modulator to generate standing ultrasonic waves at 100 MHz. Utilizing this acoustic field as a template, we fabricated a microacoustic metagrating composed of air-filled channels at this frequency, employing a polymerized silicone replica. Our two-photon lithography system achieved a lateral resolution of 1.5 µm, allowing for the creation of a metagrating with a fundamental frequency of 200 MHz. Acoustically, the device functions as a source of ultra-high-frequency sound, radiating a first-order diffraction beam at a frequency of 150 MHz. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the efficacy of using intense ultrasonic fields as a precise manufacturing guide for complex microacoustic architectures via two-photon lithography, offering a transferable strategy for the fabrication of miniaturized, high-performance sound-manipulating systems.

Anomalous diffusion, characterized by diffusion dynamics that deviate from standard Normal behavior, is widely recognized for its power-law spreading, where the position distribution follows $P(x,t)\sim t^{-\gamma/2}\mathcal{F}(x t^{1/\gamma})$ with $\mathcal{F}$ being a generic function. While the underlying mechanisms for such non-Normal behavior in diffusion remain obscure, this study investigates one specific scenario: diffusion in a medium with random permeability. In this context, a vector field $v(u)$ is defined by $v(u)=-\nabla u u + v_0 - K(u)\nabla u$, where $K(u)$ is a random permeability function. We demonstrate that selecting $v_0$ and $K(u)$ appropriately allows the diffusion process to yield any desired target distribution. Furthermore, we identify a set of permeability functions $K(u)$ that specifically result in a Cauchy distribution at any given time $t$.

This study develops novel conversational Lyapunov theorems that guarantee the existence of common quadratic Lyapunov (CQL) functions near a common equilibrium point. These results specifically address regulation systems where multiple distinct controllers produce dynamics allowing states to converge asymptotically to the equilibrium under individual operation, yet the system exhibits transient behavior when a single controller is applied. The context is non-standard because the analysis permits partial unboundedness in the controls. Proving these theorems is technically challenging due to the necessity of constructing a Lyapunov function valid across all possible trajectories and control combinations simultaneously. The proposed findings hold substantial relevance for scenarios involving hybrid or switching systems, as they facilitate the circumvention of limitations inherent in existing methods that require controls to be bounded globally.

This study introduces a deep learning framework utilizing a generative adversarial network (GAN) to reconstruct velocity fields in Rayleigh–Bénard turbulent convection from sparsely sampled data generated by high-resolution numerical simulations. The architecture comprises an unrolled measurement module and paired generator-discriminator networks. The unrolled component accurately maps the observed data onto the sparse sensing matrix, while the generator produces the corresponding full-resolution flow reconstructions. The GAN structure is trained on a dataset derived from direct numerical simulations of turbulent convection at varying Reynolds numbers. Results demonstrate that the model successfully reconstructs velocity fields across different Reynolds numbers, even for those not included in the training set, indicating strong generalization capabilities. Furthermore, the sparse sampling strategy employed ensures high signal quality, with a low reconstruction error of approximately 1.5%.

Current trustworthiness frameworks prioritize robustness against global worst-case scenarios, often neglecting real-world conditions where most inputs remain unambiguous. Consequently, models exhibit superior reliability in clear cases compared to edge cases, yet existing methods lack a mechanism to quantify this variation. Introducing an assurance metric that assesses the model's certainty across different input types, this study examines how robustness fluctuates from rare, ambiguous, and intermediate regions to ideal conditions. Furthermore, we outline an inference-driven methodology utilizing rejection sampling to map models containing large volumes of unmodeled ambiguity, presenting results that validate result confidence levels across these intrinsic environments.

Strong computational resources are essential for training large-scale Reinforcement Learning (RL) models, making the creation of unified RL testing platforms with accessible resources a critical priority. We introduce **L2Explorer**, a comprehensive environment designed to evaluate diverse RL frameworks, algorithms, and new model architectures. To achieve this, we have established a comprehensive suite of data, algorithm, and utility benchmarks. Furthermore, we address prevalent issues regarding data storage and network transmission by developing specialized solutions, including a high-performance distributed data engine and an intelligent file transfer system tailored for RL needs. Finally, we provide streamlined interfaces for the deployment and evaluation of both classic and emerging RL models. Our testing results demonstrate that L2Explorer achieves a storage cost reduction of 97.4% and accelerates transfer speeds by 235% compared to existing methods.

Declarative processes, which define their desired outcomes through logic and abstract rules, are increasingly utilized in modern programming languages. However, these languages often obscure the underlying machine instructions, creating a need for innovative debugging and monitoring strategies that operate effectively within this high-level, abstract domain. We introduce Stream supervision, an original approach that employs regular expressions to monitor and analyze the execution of declarative languages by extracting specific data from streams of input and output. We have implemented this method in Prolog and evaluated its performance across various benchmarks, demonstrating the generalizability of our methodology.

Light confined within one-dimensional photonic quasicrystal arrays undergoes a transition from localized to shifted-delocalized states, a phenomenon that mirrors the transition seen in infinite systems. We demonstrate that these photonic states retain their utility in encoding and reading out binary data, even after shifting. Additionally, we identify that the binary value decoded from the average position of the displaced states matches the same result obtained from both the original localization position and the system-wide reentrant delocalization shift.

"Liger," a new high-speed, multi-fiber optical system recently installed at the W.M. Keck Observatory, enables the simultaneous acquisition of spectra and time-domain data across three modes: 4 fibers at a 10 kHz sampling rate, 16 fibers at 100 Hz, and up to 500 fibers at 100 Hz. This document details the progress of the system's data processing architecture, which operates on a custom platform designed for the system. Key elements include the Data Acquisition Controller (DAC), the Optical Distribution Unit (ODU), and the Fiber Switch Matrix (FSM). The article outlines the electrical and optical subsystems, the ligand insertion mechanism, the vacuum environment, illumination architecture, and image processing techniques used to derive precise fiber positions and flux measurements. Furthermore, it describes the spectrum processing pipeline, which leverages the 256-channel wavelength-dispersion spectrometer and the on-board CMOS camera to process optical data. Finally, the paper presents the software framework running on the DAC, which interfaces the ODU and FSM, manages data storage, and provides the tools necessary for subsequent spectral analysis.

Multiplexing spatial modes of single-photon wavepackets enables the creation of high-density quantum image sensors, allowing for spatial resolutions that surpass the optical diffraction limit. This study introduces an experimental approach to unambiguously identify Laguerre-Gaussian spatial modes in two-photon Fock states. The results demonstrate a two-fold enhancement in the point spread function's transverse resolution when spatially encoding single photons at the diffraction limit, with the observed resolution aligning perfectly with theoretical predictions.

We examine the relationship between the algebraic compactification of parameter spaces and the Vossen compactification of generic parameter ranges, demonstrating their congruence on the set of polynomial coefficients. Furthermore, we evaluate several alternative algebraic compactifications within a specific case quadratic polynomials. Our findings indicate that the space of quadratic coefficients, when compactified, yields a structure isomorphic to the set of all parabolic complex transformations modulo affine equivalence.

Biophysical ecosystems are inherently dynamic, characterized by continuous fluctuations across multiple temporal scales ranging from brief disturbances to enduring regime shifts. While short-term variability often attracts the most attention, it is increasingly recognized that these transient states can foreshadow significant demographic restructuring. This study focuses on the North American boreal songbird population, utilizing data from the Breeding Bird Survey (1966–2016) to analyze the identification of persistent transients and detect early warning signals of substantial demographic changes. Our methodology integrates a time-scale decomposition of data variance with an analysis of the system's autocovariance structure to isolate non-decaying transient components. Our decomposition successfully isolates transients distinct from steady-state trends or cycles, a feat unattainable with standard filtering or decomposition models. We demonstrate that specific persistent transients function as early warning signals for substantial demographic shifts, specifically capturing the initial demographic decline of the American Redstart prior to its observed population collapse. Consequently, this analytical approach offers a robust framework for monitoring and forecasting demographic changes in natural populations.

The correlation between a galaxy's bulge and its main-sequence (M*-SFR) linkage is well-established, with both parameters rising together; yet, the specific mechanism driving this effect remains unclear. Using a sample of 1,000 local star-forming galaxies drawn from the SPARC bulge database and leveraging the MUSE instrument, we examined the connection between the M*-specific star-formation rate (SFR) and the stellar velocity dispersion within bulges ($\sigma_{\text{bulge}}$). We found that elevated $\sigma_{\text{bulge}}$ values correspond to higher specific SFRs, indicating that galaxy bulges experience the same physics governing the main sequence regardless of mass. However, we note that the current sample size precludes a precise determination of the functional form for this (Bulge-$\sigma$) relationship or its exact causality. Consequently, we propose that the growth of bulges serves as a proxy for the processes regulating star formation across the M*-SFR trajectory.

This study introduces two cross-lingual approaches to sentiment analysis, designed to expand the scope of research in this field. In a homogeneous setting, these methods utilize only training data from a single language, leveraging data augmentation via the proposed techniques. Conversely, the corresponding heterogenous scenarios utilize augmentation strategies to analyze target-language sentiments based on source-language training datasets. We implemented this framework using BERT-based classifiers to evaluate sentiment analysis across three datasets covering Spanish, Portuguese, and Greek. The results indicate that cross-lingual analysis is feasible, with these advanced techniques enabling the task with significantly fewer labeled examples.

This study examines the self-decorating process, where self-improvement agents modify segmentations of a unit interval based on their relative positions within specific sub-intervals. We demonstrate that when agents utilize relative rank as a metric for decoration length, the resulting system exhibits a dynamic reminiscent of "conways game of life," ultimately driving the segments toward uniform parity. In contrast, utilizing absolute position-based decoration lengths results in oscillatory patterns of expanding and contracting segments. We provide an algorithm capable of predicting the stable configuration of these segments after decoration dynamics subside.

This paper investigates the set of time $h \in (0,1)$, defined as $\mathcal{T}_h = \{t \in [0,1] : B^{\text{h}}(t) < d\}$ for a fixed $d \in \mathbb{R}$. It is established that $\mathcal{T}_h$ possesses a non-empty interior and its Hausdorff dimension equals $3h$, with its Lebesgue measure having finite and positive value.

Dirac's variational principle is employed to examine the Henon-Heiles model with quantum disorder, utilizing a single-parameter trial wave function derived via the Jackiw-Kerman formalism. While this approach accurately captures qualitative dynamics across a broad spectrum of disorder strengths, it exhibits a notable deficiency: it fails to predict a third stochastic layer, corresponding to the humped homoclinic orbit, unless the disorder intensity is increased sufficiently to destroy that chaotic layer entirely.

This study examines X-ray images of COVID-19 patients to analyze how ICU admission correlates with pulmonary infection patterns. We collected 1,000 X-ray pairs, categorizing each as indicative of ICU admission or non-ICU discharge. The data set was partitioned into separate training and testing groups. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) were employed to train the model for classifying X-rays and were subsequently used to process unseen test images. Upon generating probability scores for new X-ray inputs, we sorted the test cohort by these scores into distinct percentile ranges. For every range, we compared demographic and clinical metrics between the actual ICU admission and non-ICU discharge groups. The results demonstrate that ICU admissions are associated with more severe pulmonary involvement than non-ICU discharges. Furthermore, we identified specific score intervals where metrics such as average age, gender composition, and the count of positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR tests differed significantly. These statistical distinctions between admission outcomes within defined severity percentiles may offer valuable insights for future research.

The construction of the global simplicial bundle introduces a tool intended for use in global analysis on simplicial manifolds, functioning somewhat like the bundle of forms inverse. It enables the transition from a partition by simplexes to an associated algebra of cocycles, which carries a well-defined Chech-cocycle structure. This approach preserves critical geometric and topological attributes from the original manifold, including its homotopy groups and the associated exact sequence. Importantly, this process generates a consistent pattern of operations on the collected cocycles, resembling a "simplicial" framework, though it requires further validation to confirm these properties rigorously. As a result, investigators may reconstruct the original global arrangement of simplexes from this algebra of cocycles under suitable conditions, thereby reconstructing the initial manifold's structure.

Visual association detection (VAD) automates linking detected instances of a specific crime across numerous images, offering significant advantages in criminal investigations. Nevertheless, current VAD models frequently yield spurious detections due to issues like data leakage or domain shifts, which can mislead police by suggesting a suspect's presence in locations where they were never actually present. Although manual verification of all candidate associations is impractical, it is essential to filter out these incorrect predictions. We introduce a practical, cost-effective solution that leverages the visual content surrounding each association to identify and remove false positives. By utilizing an off-the-shelf scene-text recognition system, our approach identifies text overlays that explicitly label an association as correct, achieving a remarkable 99.5% accuracy in detecting false associations in our test dataset. This method effectively addresses a critical challenge in criminal justice, enabling the efficient processing of vast numbers of associations with high reliability.

Deep learning approaches, including those utilizing temporal convolution and recurrent units, along with transformers, have demonstrated remarkable efficacy in human action recognition. Nevertheless, these methods demand substantial amounts of data and computational power to attain high precision. To mitigate these data and computational hurdles, we introduce Delta Sampling R-Transformer (Delta Sampling R-BERT) for action recognition. This method employs delta sampling to select a sparse subset of video frames, thereby significantly cutting data storage and data transfer expenses. Furthermore, we integrate a specialized recurrent transformer architecture that leverages both a simplified recurrent structure and dilated temporal convolution to efficiently compress video inputs while preserving a diluted temporal architecture. This architecture maintains high precision even under limited data and low-light (dim) video conditions. We evaluated our approach against several baseline models across three datasets: dim-light NMS, Kinetics, and a video surveillance action dataset. Experiments confirm that our approach outperforms baseline models, particularly in scenarios involving limited data and poor lighting conditions.

Processors capable of content-addressable parallel execution represent a promising paradigm for accelerating data-centric computations. Although prior attempts have been made to implement such concepts, limited memory bandwidth and the absence of sufficient arithmetic operations have typically hindered their operational bandwidth. This study introduces three dedicated instruction set extensions designed to enable full content-addressable parallelism within standard RISC architectures. These extensions facilitate bandwidth-optimal data selection and aggregation from parallel array elements, with implementations integrated into an FPGA version of the PowerPC processor demonstrating up to a 1000% bandwidth improvement and approximately a 400% acceleration in aggregation benchmarks compared to conventional CPU methods. A practical implementation utilizing content-associative memory (CAM) arrays is provided, though the design principles are applicable to alternative associative structures as well. Furthermore, CAM availability is not a prerequisite for adapting these techniques to other FPGA environments.

This research examines a specific galaxy cluster member, identified as a high-redshift ($\sim3$) $L^*$ disk system, utilizing semi-analytic techniques to investigate connections between stellar formation history and structural development. The findings reveal that the galaxy underwent a minor accretion event, adding approximately $10^9$ solar masses, which triggered a formation burst of roughly $10^{10}$ solar masses. This event accounted for nearly half of the galaxy's total mass assembled before redshift 3. The analytical model indicates that this small accretion played a decisive role in shaping the inner disk dynamics, specifically driving the observed uneven disk asymmetry and generating a prominent central bulge component comprising about 20% of the galaxy's total mass. Consequently, the model suggests that even limited, small-scale accretion episodes can have a profound and lasting impact on both disk irregularities and bulge formation.

The texture zero hypothesis, a framework for analyzing the structure of mass matrices, has been extensively examined over recent decades. Within this study, we conduct a comprehensive global analysis of the three-generation texture zero models in both the quark and lepton sectors. By utilizing a Markov Chain Monte Carlo methodology, we perform a systematic comparison of all viable texture zero proposals, evaluating their consistency with current experimental data. Additionally, we calculate predicted values for various beyond-the-standard-model (BSM) CP-violating observables, specifically neutral-mixing box parameters and the electroweak mass ratio, which are crucial for addressing the BSM component of the cosmological matter-antimatter asymmetry known as the "global texture zero."

Current approaches to Neural Program Generation (NPG) suffer from an inability to incorporate domain-specific knowledge, frequently resulting in created code that executes incorrectly or fails entirely. To address this, we introduce a framework for Neural Program Construction (NPC), which enables the conditional generation of source code based on programming languages' syntactic and semantic rules. Within our framework, target programs are synthesized by joining code snippets from a provided pool, with join points determined dynamically by the input context. This process is governed by static constraints derived from the target language, ensuring that all outputs are statically verified. We implemented this framework in the form of a Python tool, NPC, demonstrating its practicality. Our findings show that NPC allows neural models to generate functionally correct code at a rate 30% higher than that of current neural approaches, resulting in programs that are easier to maintain.

On November 7, 2004, a Neutron Decomposition Event (NDE) occurred in the Sun, allowing the detection of an excess of protons by the Advanced Composition Experiment (ACE-LEXS) instrument. This analysis utilizes ACE-LEXS spectral data to investigate these elevated proton levels, which are hypothesized to result from the dissociation of short-lived atomic species like Hydroxyl (OH) or Hydrogen Peroxide ($H_2O_2$) generated during NDEs. By examining proton energy spectra and comparing observed excesses with simulated atomic concentrations of OH and $H_2O_2$ following such events, this study suggests that NDEs could be a viable mechanism for explaining certain ACE-LEXS readings.

The study of linearized fluctuations in relativistic viscous fluids serves a dual purpose: it facilitates the numerical simulation of heavy-ion collisions and provides indirect experimental access to non-equilibrium fluid properties, such as shear and bulk viscosity. The standard first-order theory, known as first-order (Landau-Lifshitz) fluid dynamics, yields complex, often acausal equations for these propagators. In contrast, second-order formulations offer improved causal behavior and have been supported by collision data. This work introduces a unified framework to derive second-order fluid equations based on general principles, enabling the derivation of propagators for various causal models. The study focuses on the most data-favored approach, the anisotropic Muller-Matsuda formalism, demonstrating that its associated propagators can be recast into a specific form. This reformulated structure allows the implementation of a relaxation-time approximation (RTA), which is typically used in kinetic theory. Crucially, applying RTA to this formalism results in propagators that are significantly simpler than those found in standard models, behaving effectively like first-order equations while retaining essential causal features.

This study examines whether government bodies can mandate decryption, utilizing the NIST submission for the Trellis-Whiteside (TW) standardization, which mandates a decryption interface, as a case. We demonstrate that the encryption scheme TW-128 is vulnerable to a decryption attack revealing the secret key, whereas TW-256 suffers from partial key leakage via similar means. The proposed attack on TW-128 achieves a complexity of approximately $2^{125.4}$ operations and necessitates $2^{75}$ forced decryptions, while the attack on TW-256 results in a complexity of roughly $2^{248.5}$ operations and requires $2^{194}$ forced decryptions.

This study introduces a measurement-device-independent (MDD) quantum key distribution model applicable to various error correction and privacy amplification techniques, serving as a comprehensive framework for simulating multiple MDD-KEX algorithms, including the BB84 variant, the four-state protocol, and the SARG04 protocol. While acknowledging the existence of similar simulators, we note that they often address only specific protocols; by offering a model adaptable to diverse error correction and privacy amplification algorithms, this work provides greater universality. The proposed framework has been utilized to evaluate and contrast different settings of the original BB84 protocol against their respective outcomes in practice-based configurations.

This work investigates general-weighted constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs), extending classic CSP research by examining vertex and edge-weighted variants across diverse structural contexts. We present new algorithms that leverage multiple properties—including line graphs, general polar decompositions, $\top$-free structures, and junction trees—to derive PTASes for numerous previously unresolved problems. Additionally, we introduce a unified framework grounded in the concept of general polar decompositions, unifying various recent techniques for finding near-optimum solutions in CSPs on trivalent graphs.

This study introduces a novel numerical scheme designed to handle a broad class of Fokker-Planck equations, encompassing multiple singularities in their partial differential operators, which are complemented by a locally Lipschitz continuous, possibly nonconvex Hamiltonian. The proposed method integrates a high-order Lagrange-Euler hybrid approach along with a transformation of variables. By integrating a spatial coordinate transform that regularizes the differentiated operators in the original Hamiltonian with the application of a specific cubic elevated polynomial within a finite element framework, we successfully circumvent standard convexity requirements typically imposed on the Hamiltonian. Through rigorous analysis, we demonstrate the convergence of the transformed finite element method under minimal assumptions regarding the Hamiltonian. Furthermore, the paper validates the scheme's application in the specific context of computing equilibria for the Kakeya problem within mean-field games.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have recently demonstrated remarkable performance in numerous tasks, largely owing to their ability to automatically learn hierarchical feature representations from raw data. This study focuses on the analysis, understanding, and representation of these deep architectures. We examine the interpretability of both the input and output layers. Regarding interpretation, we address the analysis of intermediate hidden layers, specifically investigating how units within these layers function as parts, objects, or patterns. Additionally, this work explores the intrinsic relationship between units across different levels of the network hierarchy.

The recent launch of the Facade mission has provided the first direct measurements of the rotation periods for the four moons of Europa, which were previously only constrained by rough estimates. Facade detected periodic Doppler shifts in the thermal infrared emissions of these moons, correlating the shifts with Europa's orbital motion. Analysis indicates that the satellite systems of both Europa and Io function as coupled rotors, with Europa driving the more massive, distant moons into synchronization. This phenomenon suggests a transfer of energy through tidal forces, yet it remains unclear whether these moons passively absorb angular momentum or initiate an as-yet-undefined mechanism to redistribute it internally.

Rapid dissemination of fake news online, bolstered by social media and the internet, poses a significant threat to public well-being and societal stability. Current detection methods often rely on heuristic or statistical techniques that fail to adequately address the complexity of fake news, particularly regarding the intricate interplay between visual and textual elements in multimodal formats. This study introduces MetaNer, the inaugural end-to-end deep learning framework dedicated to emergent fake news detection through an analysis of complex emergent patterns in visual-textual data. MetaNer integrates multiple state-of-the-art algorithms to extract visual and textual features, utilizing attention mechanisms to capture visual-textual emergent patterns. Furthermore, it employs meta-learning via pathway optimization to adapt to new datasets with minimal new data. Experiments conducted on the CLEF 2019 and 2020 Fact Extraction and Verification (FAVE) challenges demonstrate that MetaNer achieves competitive performance, with results indicating that it can effectively detect emergent counterfeit news.

The concept of Age of Knowledge (ACK), first introduced in 2014 by F. Busnies, functions as a metric for knowledge freshness, paralleling the Age of Information (AOI). While the majority of existing literature addresses point-to-point queueing channels, this paper specifically examines the ACK for a Bernoulli single-server channel characterized by one open slot and a blocking mechanism. The analysis begins with a scenario where packet arrival times remain unknown, deriving the knowledge age's probability density function (PDF) through the age of blocked packet (ABP) distribution. Subsequently, considering known knowledge arrival times, this study establishes a temporal mapping between knowledge ages and blocked packet ages to determine the knowledge age distribution. Furthermore, we analyze how knowledge age performance shifts in response to variations in channel service rates and the parameters of the knowledge arrival process.

We present a novel family of quantum group-like quasi-bialgebras, where the Drinfeld twist depends on the specific variety set-theoretic solution to the Yang-Baxter equation. In this framework, the J-map is expressed entirely in terms of the arithmetic of the solution set. We demonstrate that our model generalizes the classification provided by S. Mozgovoy and A. Schiffmann regarding set-theoretic Yang-Baxter equation solutions compatible with quantum groups lacking a Drinfeld twist. Furthermore, we introduce a specific class of symmetric set-theoretic solutions, from which we construct quantum group-like structures free of twist, thereby establishing a correspondence with the tripartite algebraic framework detailed herein. Finally, we explore the properties of these formulations when the set-theoretic solutions possess additional algebraic or graphical features.

Polyphase Golay Complementary Structures (GCS) have garnered significant attention recently due to their ability to produce sum sidelobes that are essentially zero, making them highly valuable for applications like multitone synchronization and radar design. This paper reviews the primary developments in constructing complex GCS with large dimensions. It begins by detailing the foundational definitions and properties of these structures along various design methodologies, including those for small sizes. Furthermore, it focuses extensively on the design of complex GCS with large orders, elaborating in detail on the recent discovery of a design formula for specific 4-nomial coefficients.

Silicon stands as a leading candidate for integrating quantum dots into scalable quantum computing architectures. This study examines the deployment of silicon-embedded valence bond defects (VBDs) to facilitate spin-state manipulation of resident electrons and holes using mid-infrared photons. We present initial findings on spin-dependent tunneling between a quantum dot and a single-site VBD within silicon, demonstrating the capability to alter valley populations and execute arbitrary single-qubit operations on both electrons and holes. Furthermore, we report the generation of a spin-dependent spin current, suggesting that atom-scale silicon spintronics could form the foundation for efficient quantum interconnects between quantum processors.

Deep learning architectures, particularly Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), have recently demonstrated remarkable efficacy in processing graph-structured data. This capability enables precise predictions on tasks such as drug candidate assessment, material property analysis, and credit risk determination. In this paper, we examine the application of deep learning to simulate and forecast the evolution of dynamical systems. We hypothesize that by training a GNN to predict the immediate state changes of constituent elements based on their interactions, the network implicitly masters the underlying system dynamics. Consequently, the learned graph-based models are capable of accurately emulating long-term behavioral trajectories. Furthermore, we investigate the integration of evolutionary graph structures to capture systemic evolution over time. Our findings indicate that these approaches yield significant advantages in both computational efficiency and data efficiency. Specifically, a graph-based model requiring only 100 time-step predictions per node can reliably simulate systems with dynamics extending up to $10^9$ time-steps. Additionally, this methodology proves versatile, successfully handling diverse domains ranging from neural circuit behavior and epidemiological spread to financial market fluctuations.

We introduce a general framework for infinite monoids equipped with polynomial growth, applying it to analyze the structure of partitions found in stable homotopy theory. Specifically, we determine an explicit formula for $| \pi_n(\mathbb{Z}/p\text{Spin})|$ for all n and primes, thereby resolving a question originally raised by Rognes.

To support training models for neuro-debilitating disease diagnosis, generating large-scale annotated datasets is essential. However, acquiring such data remains costly and labor-intensive. While current adversarial variation auto-encoders (VAE) have demonstrated the ability to create diverse and realistic MRI lesions, their use for generating multiple distinct disease types requires numerous separate networks. To address this limitation, we introduce a unified Progressive Adversarial Variational auto-encoder (Progressive VAE). This framework employs a single network architecture to generate multiple types of cerebral lesions, eliminating the need for the overhead associated with maintaining multiple networks. Our method conditions the base VAE using three elements: the specific target disease category, a z-vector sampled from a standard normal distribution, and high-resolution partial healthy MRI slices. These inputs guide the primary generator, which produces low-resolution symmetric images that are subsequently upsampled into high-resolution outputs. Symmetry is guaranteed by upsample patterns, while progressive enhancement ensures structural fidelity. To further refine realism and tissue characteristics, we employ two discriminators focused on global image structure and specific disease attributes, respectively. This conditioning strategy allows the base generator to function efficiently across various pathologies with only minor adjustments, effectively handling the complexities of multi-disease generation. Experiments utilizing MRI data from five distinct diseases confirm that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both synthetic image quality and its utility for data augmentation in clinical machine learning applications.

Quantum entanglement serves as a fundamental resource for nonlocality, which facilitates tasks such as distinguishing orthogonal quantum states more effectively than any classical strategy. This research examines robust quantum nonlocality within specific families of unextendable product bases (UPBs), demonstrating that single-state perturbations allow for such distinction via measurement-dependent teleportation utilizing only quantum resources. Initially, we establish quantum nonlocality for UPBs in bipartite systems with dimensions $3\times 3$ and $3\times 4$. Subsequently, we prove the existence of robust quantum nonlocality for specific UPBs across several systems, including $3\times 3$, $3\times 4$, $3\times 5$, and $3\times 6$ configurations. Finally, we introduce a general criterion to ascertain this robustness for arbitrary UPBs within any given system.

Data for the fifth phase of the Five-Star Collection project (SDSS-V astrobots) rely on two robots stationed in the optical spectrograph room to automate target acquisition and instrument control. This research examines the data integrity provided by the precise mutual clocking mechanism between the robots. Experiments were conducted in an unobstructed environment to analyze the synchronization performance of the collection V project's data.

Originally introduced in 1999, the GP 2 (General Purpose 2) compiler for the HSPC hardware description language has consistently supported the simulation and verification efforts of researchers and industry professionals. Nevertheless, given the simulation demands of increasingly intricate System-on-Chip designs, there is a pressing requirement to boost the performance of the GP 2 preprocessor and compiler. This paper presents the significant upgrades implemented in the GP 2 compiler for GPSC 2019. By examining the specific characteristics of GP 2's preprocessor and compiler phases, this study highlights the strategies employed to enhance their execution speeds.

Recently, significant progress has been made in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, largely due to the widespread adoption of pre-trained language models (LMs) and their associated fine-tuning techniques. Although these models have proven effective for named entity recognition (NER), they have not yet demonstrated comparable utility for general attribute extraction (AE). AE entails identifying all entities matching a specific pattern or semantic class within an sentence—for example, extracting every U.S. president's name, although such patterns exist for U.S president names, though often not for other topics like product features. We introduce a novel framework that integrates representation learning with task-specific objectives to create specialized AE models. Our approach involves constructing task-oriented contrastive learning objectives, which simultaneously refine both task-related and representation components. We applied this method to three distinct AE tasks: U.S president names, although often not for other topics like product features. This paper introduces a new class of infinite collections of star normal quotient networks characterized by a twisted wreath structure, specifically defined where an infinite group $G$ is partitioned into two subgroups, $A$ and $B$, with $A$ being countable. For any function $f: A \to B$, the constructed group $E_f$ satisfies the required criteria to form such a collection within the broader framework of quotient networks. Additionally, the authors fully characterize these twisted wreath-type groups $E_f$ necessary for $E_f$ to be a normal quotient network of $S_G$. The research further explores the existence of multiple distinct normal collections for the constructed group $E_f$. Finally, the paper identifies $E_f$ as a normal subgroup within the larger group $F_G$, formed by all normal quotient network representatives of $S_G$ that are generated through functions from this specific partitioned family.

Categorical variables are frequently encountered in both research and practical applications within the realm of high-dimensional data analysis, yet they present unique modeling challenges. In this work, we introduce a novel penalized regression framework designed to address categorical predictors in high-dimensional settings. By integrating the precalculated contrasts between categories into the penalty term, we enforce sparsity on individual categories. We demonstrate that our proposed method achieves optimal performance by attaining the minimax rate under squared error loss. Furthermore, we establish its superior efficacy in outperforming existing approaches through various numerical experiments.

Extending pre-trained language models (LMs) with more parameters often boosts performance but risks diminishing returns and significant additional computational costs. We introduce an improved strategy for bottom-up distillation designed to extend LMs effectively. Our approach streamlines the teacher student relationship by structuring the training process to focus on specific layers, ensuring a more organized knowledge transfer. Our method, called Skill (Illustration of Extending LMs via Extensible Learning), allows for flexible expansion of LMs while maintaining performance and reducing overhead. By organizing the training process into structured layers, we ensure that the model learns efficiently from its teacher counterpart. Our experiments confirm that Skill allows students to expand LMs with better performance and lower costs.

We introduce new nonlocal diffusion frameworks applicable to both subdiffusion ($\alpha \in (0,2)$) and superdiffusion ($\alpha \in (0,\infty)$) that yield coherent local and fractional operators depending on coherent fractional limits for diffusion processes. By utilizing a nonlocal state variable to integrate historical path data through one-sided or local fractional integration of order $\beta = \alpha - s$—where $s$ represents the fractional order of the process—we achieve agreement with either the local or a specific variant of fractional description for movement regularity. These approaches provide a spectrum of sub- or superdiffusive behaviors with a single nonlocal framework, as well as a continuity between fractional local and nonlocal operators.

This letter introduces two methods for generating panoramic stitchings from a camera's gravity orientation. These methods are particularly useful for creating virtual reality experiences, such as medical procedures, where retaining the device's real-world orientation is essential. Two specific approaches are proposed: one utilizing a roll-pitch-yaw (RPY) rotation to align the roll axis with gravity, and another employing a linear transformation through a derived transformation matrix. Both techniques effectively achieve panoramic stitching based on this gravity-aligned preference.

The paper investigates the combinatorial aspects required for removing poles of certain non-holomorphic Eisenstein series, specifically those linked to the Borel subgroup of $GL(n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$. Its primary objective is to present a new formula for the residue of these Eisenstein series, which is valid for all relevant rank-1 parabolic subgroups. To achieve this, the work builds upon established results by Cogdell, Piatetski-Shapiro, and Shahidi, while introducing an explicit, explicit combinatorial description of the Rostand–Solé–Shahadi (2006) integral, specifically the local zeta function involved, as developed in the current work.

Although Parkinson's disease is the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder globally, the absence of a validated biophysical computational model hinders the optimization of therapeutic strategies. Using detailed single-cell and in vivo imaging datasets from marmoset primates, we developed a novel biophysical model of the striatum. This model accounts for the electrical characteristics of neurons, morphological structures, and complex circuit-level interactions, with parameters derived directly from experimental data through statistical optimization. A primary achievement of this work is the successful integration of morphologically realistic models for both spiny projection neurons and interneurons, along with experimentally grounded models of neuronal morphology and ion channels, into a cohesive computational framework. Model simulations effectively replicate the physiological and pathological electrophysiological and imaging biomarkers observed in striatal disorders associated with Parkinson's disease, including changes in neuronal firing rates, rate adaptation, calcium spike patterns, and the pathological shifts in low-frequency oscillations characteristic of the condition. Furthermore, the model accurately reproduces the therapeutic outcomes of deep brain stimulation (DBS) as seen in primates, providing insights into the specific mechanisms underlying both disease pathology and treatment efficacy. Ultimately, this model represents a crucial advancement in biophysical approaches, potentially facilitating future investigations into the mechanisms of Parkinson's disease and the refinement of related therapies.

Line connections in road maps often suffer from spatial anti-aliasing artifacts at their junctions due to the discrete sampling nature of computer screens. While existing solutions address single lines individually, they frequently fail to ensure visual consistency where lines meet. This study introduces an anti-aliasing framework specifically designed for line junctions in vector-based map rendering. By analytically deriving the one-dimensional projection of two-line junctions in space, the proposed method calculates precise color values directly in the stroke area without relying on traditional blur techniques. Results indicate that this approach yields visually superior line junctions with enhanced rendering performance. Additionally, the analysis of line junction projections offers a general method for rendering precise line ends, applicable broadly to scenarios where lines terminate against background boundaries.

We present IFU observations of nine units or pairs of ultra/luminous infrared galaxies (U/LIRGs) selected from the Great Observatories All-Sky LIRG Survey (GOALS) using the KOOLS-IFU integral field spectrograph attached to the Seimei Telescope. The dataset encompasses narrow- and broad-band photometry, multi-wavelength classifications, galaxy morphologies, ionized gas properties, and kinematic structures. The sample was chosen based on the availability of H$\beta$ emission lines and the KOOLS-IFU's narrow-band filters, covering a redshift range of z < 0.04. The primary results indicate the spatial distribution of ionized gas ionization, the prevalence of non-gravitational dynamics, and the alignment of ionization orientations with non-kinematic vectors. The data reveals that ionization conditions vary among different galaxies, with most exhibiting mixed ionization signatures. The observed non-gas dynamics are likely driven by outflows associated with active galactic nuclei (AGN) or major starbursts. The alignment between ionization features and non-kinematic vectors implies that AGN and starburst activities are widespread in the GOALS sample. The primary limitation of the study is the narrow field of view, which restricts the detection of accretion and outflows in the majority of targets.
