We examine the factorization of exclusive meson distributions and fragmentation in the dYan process and B-meson decays, utilizing twist-3 quark and quark-antiquark correlations alongside twist-3 gluus polarizations. This study addresses the inherent ambiguities in quark distribution functions and the convergence issues associated with series summation. Our methodology involves reinterpreting these exclusive processes as the initial- or final-state limits of deep inelastic scattering with photon-proton collisions, and quark-antiquark annihilation, respectively. This approach facilitates the integration of quark distributions into their standard factorization framework, thereby resolving the convergence challenges for the associated series.

Magnetic and electronic symmetries are fundamental to understanding material behavior, yet determining them from first principles within large unit cells is notoriously difficult. This study introduces an ab initio tight-binding (TB) model for every atomistic simulation, enabling the efficient evaluation of various symmetries. Leveraging recent advances in machine learning, we achieve rapid fitting of TB parameters with high accuracy using atomic positions and electronegativity data derived from standard force-field methods. Consequently, the resulting models remain sufficiently precise to correctly determine symmetry properties. We demonstrate this approach on two complex cases: a 100-atom system where we identify the magnetic ordering, and a 196-atom system where we calculate the complete electronic band structure and establish the corresponding space and point groups.

Holographic error correction schemes have been shown to support the storage of quantum states with low logical error rates, even amidst substantial and varying physical noise. This study investigates the use of hyper-invariant MERA (h-MERA), an isotropic, multi-layered holographic tensor network where associations follow a power law, to address general, stochastic noise. We demonstrate that h-MERA supports efficient error-correcting syndromes for multiple types of local noise operators. Furthermore, by leveraging the self-similar structure of Hh-MERA, we introduce a hierarchical error correction strategy capable of handling stochastic noise with a fidelity approaching that of standard MERA at equivalent parameters. We propose a specific implementation using Chebyshev Hamiltonians and verify through simulation that this scheme achieves a logical fidelity exceeding 99.99% for random 2D noise on a 2D h-MERA with a 1000-layer depth.

Driven by a periodic light field, a two-state molecular system reaches a non-equilibrium state where a balance exists between the rates of driven unimolecular isomerization and thermal back-isomerization, characterized by a distinct level of parametric susceptibility. In this study, we introduce a simplified quantum mechanical model for a rhodopsin-assisted retinal chromophore, utilizing it to investigate the dynamics of photoisomerization and thermal relaxation. Our model explicitly incorporates a dissipative mechanism that selectively promotes quantum decoherence along the excited-state reaction coordinate. Through numerical analysis, we demonstrate that the steady-state population of the molecular dimer exhibits highly sensitive dependence on both the intensity and phase of the laser driving field, as well as the ambient temperature. Furthermore, we find that the long-term molecular state can be toggled via a single photon, inducing a transition probability exceeding 50% relative to the thermal equilibrium level. Finally, we explore how various forms of environmental noise modulate these response characteristics.

Process mining has grown significantly as a data-driven methodology for analyzing Business Process Management, facilitating the visualization of workflows, the detection of anomalies, and the generation of workflow models from empirical event logs. While various machine-learning algorithms have been integrated into this field, there remains a lack of comprehensive evaluation of their collective efficacy in these applications. This paper proposes a systematic assessment of deep-learning models, categorizing them into three groups: those reconstructing workflow models from logs, those identifying process variants, and those forecasting subsequent activities within an event log context. The study evaluates these methods using a benchmark dataset derived from the IBM Federal e-Service case, which is widely utilized in process mining literature. The paper further introduces a novel deep-learning approach tailored for the discovery of process models. Finally, it offers a comprehensive examination of deep-learning limitations specific to process mining, including necessary future research avenues.

This study examines the impact of the 20.11.2020 magnitude 6.7 earthquake in Izmir, Turkey, on Twitter activity. Using the Twitter API v2, we gathered a dataset of approximately 13,000 tweets, which formed the basis for our analysis. We calculated the tweet emission rate to detect temporal patterns, identified the most active geographic regions, and performed a word frequency analysis to reveal prevalent themes within the social media data.

This study offers fresh, accessible proofs of the well-known characterization of Gelfand-Shilov spaces $S_s(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for $s \in (0,1)$, demonstrating that a Schwartz function $f$ belongs to $S_s(\mathbb{R}^n)$ if and only if its Fourier transform $\widehat{f}$ does. The authors further examine the derivative properties of these spaces and establish the continuity of various classes of Toeplitz operators acting on Gelfand-Shilov spaces.

The 2020 October 12 giant outburst of the symbiotic star AD Leo, which concluded on October 13, was preceded by a massive eruption on April 12, 1985, that mirrored it closely. This study utilizes a one-dimensional, time-dependent hydrodynamic code to generate continuum simulations of the April 1985 event, employing spectral line features observed from that time and the similar 2020 eruption as constraints. The resulting synthetic light curves across various UV bands align well with the observed AD Leo data, confirming that the April 1985 outburst served as a near-identical historical analogue to the 2020 event.

This study investigates wave transmission, unidirectional transmission, bidirectional transmission, and transmissionless states within finite periodic parity-time (PT)-symmetric waveguide networks. We present analytical methods to determine transmission coefficients and the conditions required for transmissionless states. Specifically, we identify the criteria for both coherent transmissionless states and lasing states that manifest as either bidirectional or directional outputs. The analysis covers transmission characteristics across various local potentials, including those with purely imaginary (anti-PT-symmetric) values, which support transmissionless and lasing states under specific configurations. A key mechanism identified is that transmissionless states arise when the global topological phase equals zero, a condition achieved when the local topological phase remains constant throughout the guide. Conversely, varying the local topological phase allows tuning of the global phase to achieve these states; notably, a local phase jump of $\pi$ results in a local phase shift of $\pi$, thereby fixing the global topological phase. The document further explores how transmissionless states transition into lasing states as the local potential evolves along the path from time-reversal-symmetric to time-reversal-symmetric configurations. Additionally, the work examines the relationship between transmissionless states and topological modes in finite periodic PT-symmetric waveguides.

We introduce an analysis of the dynamical behavior within a sparse, node- and self-interactions-inclusive logical network, providing exact formulas for the probabilities of its stable configurations. These formulas are applicable to the calculation of average components in the network, offering insights into the behavior of sparse Boolean models used in genetic regulation. We determine the conditions required for the network's sparse assumptions to hold and derive the probabilities of self-loops and specific interaction types, such as activation or repression. The paper also explores the conditions under which the network undergoes a density transition, deriving formulas for the transition parameter $\alpha$ and the transition probability $p_c(\alpha)$. Finally, we investigate the conditions under which the network converges to a dense state, determining $\alpha$ values and the probability $p_c(\alpha)$ to ensure convergence to a sparse state.

Superconducting theories stand as the leading framework for explaining the properties of nuclear ground states. Within this approach, the concept of superconductivity is generalized to include orbital angular momentum, involving the pairing of nucleons across different states characterized by magnetic quantum numbers $m$ and $-m$. Such a broad model relies heavily on the ability to efficiently calculate the energy of arbitrary HFB multi-quasiparticle states, a task that demands the evaluation of specific matrix elements. This work evaluates the computational effort required to determine the matrices for single-particle and two-particle operators acting between HFB configurations. The total operations count for operator types with a single operator label is found to be $16N^2+20N$, while for those with two labels, it rises to $64N^2+100N$, where $N$ represents the dimensionality of the operator space. These formulas apply regardless of the specific pairing between operator spaces and the number of unpaired particles in the HFB state. Furthermore, this study examines the calculation of expectation values for single and two-body operators in arbitrary HFB multi-quasiparticle states.

Point cloud models utilizing voxelization and volume rendering achieve robustness against variations in viewpoint, lighting, and other environmental elements. However, this environmental assimilation introduces ambiguity regarding object geometry, resulting in degraded recognition accuracy. To address this, this paper presents TPC, a transformer-based point cloud representation model that implements representation smoothing dependent on the transformation matrix. TPC employs two distinct transformation matrix–aware encoders to produce enhanced point features: the first integrates rotation-invariant descriptors with rotation-sensitive ones to incorporate environmental information selectively, while the second fuses point attributes with structural neighborhood contexts. Extensive testing across multiple object categories confirms that TPC surpasses current top-tier methods in object recognition accuracy.

This study examines communication protocols utilizing FMCW radar as a medium-access mechanism, specifically analyzing both slotted ALOHA and CSMA in radar contexts. We begin with the radar fundamentals required to understand the proposed access strategies. Subsequently, slotted ALOHA principles are adapted for radar systems, while the operation of CSMA is explained within this environment. Finally, a comparative assessment of the two protocols is provided to offer insights into their respective advantages and disadvantages.

Temporal knowledge graph completion serves as a fundamental task in knowledge graph reasoning, aiming to infer missing entries by leveraging temporal patterns within the graph. Despite the widespread success of existing methods in capturing temporal dynamics, they often neglect structural patterns in the knowledge graph. Furthermore, many approaches rely on rigid, method-specific representations that constrain their ability to adapt to diverse methodologies. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a unified framework for temporal knowledge graph inference that employs low-rank and model-independent representations. This framework incorporates sophisticated temporal encodings, including first- and higher-order temporal embeddings, as well as a model-independent encoding scheme. Within this setup, we introduce a novel temporal pattern-inductive encoding method designed to capture temporal structures in a manner compatible with arbitrary graph neural networks. We replace a rigid architecture with flexible low-rank matrix encoding to achieve model independence. This method is applicable to various graph neural networks without requiring retraining or parameter adjustment. Extensive experiments conducted on two real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both transductive and inductive inference settings.

Within the RPA framework, the complex eigen-energies associated with the giant dipole resonance in $^{16}$O are analyzed using a Jost function derived from the RPA matrix via Rumer decomposition. The results reveal that the RPA ground state exhibits multiple pairs of complex RPA roots in close proximity to real roots, a phenomenon attributed to the non-Hermiticity of the RPA matrix resulting from the inclusion of the RPA residual operator's phonon coupling term. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the primary complex root pair aligns well with experimental data and is determined chiefly by the corresponding complex elements of the RPA matrix nearest to reality. Consequently, secondary complex roots exert a negligible influence on the calculated strength function and can be disregarded. The findings also indicate that the simplified SMM model, which relies on a single SMM root pair, effectively approximates the dominant SMM elements responsible for the main resonance features.

Impact-based clustering groups states that yield similar system behaviors, enabling the aggregation of states into "impact basins" for efficient analysis. This approach has been widely utilized in ANM techniques to locate and examine clusters of unstable periodic orbits (UPOs). Traditional impact-based methods depend on an importance metric to assess the significance of a trajectory, yet no universal measure exists for all dynamical systems. Moreover, existing metrics often prioritize local basin properties over global system dynamics, potentially overlooking UP O s within basins of measure zero that still exert substantial influence on overall behavior.

To address these limitations, we propose a novel, data-driven impact-based clustering strategy designed to complement existing symmetric continuation (SC) frameworks. Our method leverages data from the catalog of UP O s generated by SC to refine the definition of the impact function. By iteratively adjusting weights through a machine-learning classifier trained on trajectory data, we distinguish between locally insignificant orbits and those possessing notable systemic effects. Our results demonstrate that these computationally derived impacts successfully identify up O s within measure-zero regions that exhibit profound overall influence on the system dynamics.

Current approaches to automatic writing, including those utilizing Recurrent Neural Networks, often rely on probability distributions derived from training data to select the next character. The primary challenge in confirming panspermia lies in distinguishing it from spontaneous extraterrestrial life origins, a task complicated by the difficulty of knowing the precise probability of independent abiogenesis events. While scalar field theory upends the traditional extremal discharge process in flat space, making it impossible to sustain a charge state with $q^2 \leqq M$, such states do exist within an anti-de Sitter background. Specifically, both flat and de Sitter/anti-de Sitter/flat spaces allow for the definition of extremal and near-extremal charged black holes, where feeble cosmic censorship is preserved by ensuring the final charge-to-mass ratio satisfies $(q_f/M_f)^2 \leqq 4$. Calculations show that for fixed final mass $M_f$, the extremal state in an AdS background supports a higher final charge $q_f$ than in flat space. Furthermore, specific variations in initial charge and final mass demonstrate that the system evolves in accordance with the first and second laws of thermodynamics.

We present paraconsistent and paracomplete variants of Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory, grounded in a many-valued logical framework utilizing a many-sorted many-sheaf interpretation. These structures are validated by models where the underlying base topos is the category of G-sets for a group G, with the specific choice of many-sorted many-sheaf semantics determined by how group actions distribute. This theoretical framework enables the exploration of distinct semantic behaviors inherent to many-valued logic, leading us to propose specific many-sorted many-sheaf models that serve as concrete semantics for both paraconsistent and paracomplete set theory.

Neural interfaces capable of deciphering gait parameters from intraneural or semi-intraneural recordings hold significant potential for developing advanced neuroprosthetics that generate highly realistic movements. This research presents the development of an algorithm designed to detect and extract ambulatory states and step frequencies from high-density electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals, obtained via a high-channel count ECoG system implanted on the primary motor cortex. Data was collected from five individuals performing various ambulatory activities, including walking at different speeds, climbing stairs, and using stair-lifting prosthetics. Preprocessing steps involved removing line-frequency noise and decimating the ECoG data to 1 Hz. Subsequently, spectral power was calculated across 1-second sliding windows using Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) analysis. An adaptive threshold technique was employed to differentiate ambulation from non-ambulation based on aggregate spectral power, while step timing was determined by identifying peaks in the power spectrum after applying a bandpass filter ranging from 0.5 to 25 Hz. These steps were confirmed visually through spectrogram analysis. The resulting adaptive detection method demonstrated high reliability, achieving a Cohen’s Kappa of 0.85 when validated against video observations. Detected step frequencies were found to closely align with those derived from video analysis, exhibiting a coefficient of variation of only 0.04. Bayesian inference relies heavily on evaluating the evidence integral, a factor also essential for computing various other integrals within statistical mechanics. Although traditional methods like Monte Carlo importance sampling and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) are commonly employed to solve these, they often fail when dealing with highly complex, multi-modal, or rugged landscapes. Nested Sampling (NS), initially devised specifically for the evidence integral, offers a pathway to address such challenges; however, its application to general-purpose statistics has remained largely unexplored. This study demonstrates that NS is effectively capable of determining multiple integrals simultaneously. We validate this approach across several well-known benchmarks, including the "Four Corners" problem, spin glass models, Ising models, and the estimation of the Higgs signal strength, confirming its capability to handle intricate probability surfaces.

If the right-angled Artin group is defined by a right-angled group that arises as divisors of a right-angled Artit group, the divisors are defined by a subgraph of the generating graph. Specifically, a right-angled Artit group $A(\Gamma')$ is a divisor of $A(\Psi)$ exactly when there exists a subgraph $\Lambda \subseteq \Psi$ (which is also right-angled) such that the isomorphism class of $A(\Lambda)$ matches $A(\Psi')$.

Graphical models offer a robust mathematical framework for analyzing complex multivariate dynamic systems, yet their practical application is hindered by the computational difficulty of graphical model selection. To address this, we introduce Deep Dynamic Efficient Connectivity (DDEC), a novel graphical model selection method designed to capture time-varying dependencies among nodes in temporal series data. Leveraging the assumption of short-term dynamics modeled as latent linear processes, we employ a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) to achieve highly efficient estimation of dynamic connectivity. We evaluated the model using both simulated datasets and recordings from a spiking neural network implementing a chaotic Lorenz attractor, demonstrating that the model is capable of precisely reconstructing the underlying latent dynamic structure. Furthermore, despite its linear parameter count relative to the time series' dimensionality, we utilized a long-short term memory (LSTM)-based classifier to train on extracted dynamic connectivity features for the task of state reconstruction, successfully classifying the system states.

Phylogenetic networks serve as evolutionary models capable of depicting both evolutionary tree segments and non-tree processes, such as horizontal gene transfer, gene fusion, and gene duplication. By computationally deriving these networks from genomic or phylogenetic tree data—and possibly supplementing them with user input—researchers can execute downstream analyses involving gene classification and the addition of reticulation nodes (like those representing horizontal transfer). We evaluated and compared the architectures of current phylogenetic network software, discovering that only limited commonalities exist among the numerous existing approaches for network generation. Consequently, we propose a modular framework designed to standardize creator components and address this deficiency. Accompanying this structure is an open-source implementation, pNNC ("phylogenetic Network Network Creator"), which unifies various existing network generators into a single package. This tool also incorporates optimizations for performance and accessibility, including support for massive datasets containing millions of taxa, interactive visualization via the Web, and containerized deployment through Docker.

Monitoring the motion of living organisms in video footage is a fundamental task with wide-ranging applications, from tracking insects in nature documentaries to observing livestock in agricultural contexts. While prior work has developed tools for image-based movement detection, existing approaches often depend on specialized training data, such as insect-specific models, or on human-annotated landmarks like leg tips. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces a novel, general-purpose computational algorithm that identifies movement through generic physiological characteristics. By analyzing how living entities consume energy to maintain motion, this method distinguishes biological activity from static objects like plastic models or wind-driven leaves, even in the absence of trained models, manual labels, or clear body part definitions. The proposed approach was rigorously evaluated on two distinct datasets: a collection of one hundred uncurated YouTube home videos and a group of twelve expertly annotated research sequences. Expert annotators assessed both expert-level and novice-level annotators on the video samples. Previous work by the authors identified scattering regimes where absorption eigenchannels acquire real summities. In this study, we broaden these findings to cover both open and closed eigenchannels across general sum-allowed interactions. We demonstrate that these results follow necessarily from the unitarity of non-unitary interaction theories. Furthermore, we present numerical evidence indicating these principles apply to the Yukawa potential and selected repulsive interactions. Notably, our research reveals a direct connection between these summities and recent observations regarding the duality of absorption resonances and bound states within non-unitary systems.

We examine one-loop generation of the Higgs boson mass in the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model by explicitly deriving the relevant mass matrix elements and the Higgs self-coupling from a hypercomplex non-minimal Higgs sector in the scalar potential, utilizing a hyperquaternions auxiliary field approach. This method yields a model-parameterized effective Higgs self-coupling expressed as a function of top-quark Yukawa, $\tan\beta$, and $m_T$, defined by the sum of the scalar and trilinear top-scalar interactions. We investigate the dependence of this self-coupling on these specific parameters and utilize the loop-induced Higgs mass formula to analyze how the real parts of the stops' complex mass eigenvalues and the staus' mass eigenvalues contribute to the on-shell Higgs mass.

This study examines linespelling assessment for neural network auto-regressive (NAR) models used in forecasting single-indexed time series. We evaluate two methods for measuring linearity: the universal approximation property and the distance-based residual test. A universal model capable of replicating any stochastic process with zero mean and finite variance possesses the universal approximation property. In contrast, the distance-based residual test measures linearity by calculating the prediction errors of such universal models applied specifically to the given time series data. We illustrate these approaches using both simulated datasets and a case study forecasting the Shanghai Composite Stock Price Index.

Dynamic cell processes, such as migration and the migration of membrane proteins, are driven by interactions among complex biophysical mechanisms. To study these phenomena, researchers require advanced simulation tools. We introduce a novel framework designed to model the combined effects of cell motility, protein migration within membranes, and overall hydrodynamic interactions. This approach addresses both the non-Newtonian rheology of the cytoplasmic fluid and the external environment, as well as the cell's structure, by utilizing a hybrid method. This method couples a coarse-grained approach for the cell and surrounding fluid with a multiphase front-tracking technique to capture the interface between the cell and fluid. Our system incorporates various biological factors, including membrane and cytoskeletal tension, adhesion forces, and the Brownian motion of proteins. By integrating this versatile framework, we establish a robust foundation for investigating the migration of cells and the rearrangement of proteins within their lipid membranes under diverse, non-ideal, and physically realistic conditions.

The cryptocurrency ecosystem has enabled users to circumvent sanctions by utilizing complex, multi-hop transaction routes to mask their digital identities and obscure funds on the blockchain. While these technologies offer users anonymity, they simultaneously hinder the ability of law enforcement to conduct investigations and recover stolen assets. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel framework designed to identify illicit activity within the cryptocurrency network by automatically synthesizing executable search programs from natural language hints. These logic-based search terms enable law enforcement to efficiently recover cryptocurrency assets. Our framework operates within the blockchain environment to recover funds derived from known sanctions violations, such as those involving blacklisted wallet addresses. We validated our system using a live test case involving the recovery of Bitcoin stolen from a sanctioned Ethereum address, successfully recovering 0.015 BTC (approximately $1,000 USD) by tracing funds through a multi-hop wallet address.

Topological quantum computation (TQC) offers a pathway to fault-resilient computing by executing logical operations through the braiding of anyons, with measurement occurring via their fusion. Although this approach relies on complex hardware, its software can be significantly simplified by leveraging the intrinsic fault-resilience of topological systems. A primary hurdle in TQC is the non-local nature of topological measurements, which necessitates error correction that must contend with both environmental noise and calculation-intrinsic faults. This challenge is further compounded by the difficulty in executing fault-resilient braiding operations when the number of required qubits increases. This study introduces a reinforcement learning framework designed to execute topological braiding automatically, where the agents receive rewards based on the successful realization of fault-resilience conditions. We applied our method to the double-semion model and demonstrated that a near-optimal policy emerges after approximately 100 total braiding executions. Under this optimal strategy, the learning process involves no parameter tuning and does not require prior knowledge of the system's topological structure.

In quantum metrology, employing a single qubit as a probe enables a quantization limit where precision scales as $1/ \sqrt{t}$ with a scaling factor of $2$ in the probe number within each cavity. This work demonstrates the implementation of quantum-enhanced metrology using two qubits distributed across separate cavities to precisely measure field phases. Under specific conditions, this setup achieves quantum scaling for phase variance, reaching a magnitude of $5$ times the quantum classical standard. Furthermore, by integrating decoherence-suppression strategies, the system attains quantum scaling even beyond regimes exceeding initial operational boundaries.

This study examines how jets interact with the medium by analyzing direct photon-hadron distributions. By leveraging the photon's lack of color charge, this approach offers a robust method to probe jet quenching, allowing researchers to isolate medium effects from intrinsic non-perturbative and higher-order perturbative contributions through comparison with theoretical models. The analysis utilizes direct photon-hadron data collected in Au+Au and d+Au collisions at the LHC, presenting results from two distinct impact parameter regimes: central Au+Au and d+Au events at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=200$ GeV. The central Au+Au section features a significant medium, whereas the d+Au section features a significantly less dense or absent one. The dataset spans a wide range of photon transverse momenta ($p_{T}^{\gamma}$), extending from 5 to 50 GeV/c. Theoretical predictions are generated using the JEWEL and MARTINI frameworks, which incorporate various mechanisms for jet-medium interactions. The analysis highlights a pronounced jet "shadowing" effect in both the central and d+Au d+Au scenarios, characterized by a suppression of hadrons at low $p_{T}^{\text{had}}$ relative to the photon partner. This suppression is notably more intense in the d+Au collisions, suggesting that the observed phenomenon may stem from mechanisms other than pure jet quenching. Investigated are properties of $S(n)$, and it is demonstrated that for any positive integer $k$, the equation $S(n) = k$ possesses infinitely many solutions. Additionally, the average order and asymptotic behavior of $S(n)$ are established.

This paper examines how network efficiency variability, originating from competing traffic, influences the scalability of scientific applications. As scientific workloads increasingly utilize available network capacity, they become susceptible to interference. We introduce a methodology that integrates application-specific metrics with network behavior analysis to evaluate these effects. By applying this approach to two HPC benchmarks—MPC and molecular dynamics simulations—we investigate the sensitivity of applications to such variability. Using runtime profiling and performance counters, we analyze how different network loads affect performance, with a specific focus on variability. Our findings reveal that application scalability is significantly compromised when efficiency fluctuates, causing performance degradation that exceeds that of steady-state conditions matching the average available link efficiency. Furthermore, we demonstrate that applications react uniquely to these fluctuations, indicating the necessity for application-centric testing under variable network conditions.

In this paper, we examine the distributed learning framework for the multi-armed bandit problem within a network of agents situated in shared environments. A key feature of our model is a scenario where a central situation generator assigns tasks to two types of learners—honest and corrupted—based on a secret random setting unknown to any individual agent. This model incorporates an adversary capable of tampering with a limited number of arms to influence decision-making. Crucially, we propose a learning protocol operating in an environment where agents cannot reveal their private configurations to one another. Under these constraints, we demonstrate that honest participants can still recover the optimal strategy at a learning rate matching that of a noise-free, centralized setup. In contrast, the performance of the system degrades when facing an adversary, yet remains secure provided the number of fraudulent arms is sufficiently limited.

In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, software development has shifted predominantly to remote work, prompting researchers to investigate its effects on work-life balance, stress, and team dynamics. This paper examines whether remote working influences the success of projects managed under the Scrum framework. This shift in focus is timely, prompting the Scrum Guide to include "working from home" as an example of flexible environments. To explore these effects, the authors conducted a mixed-methods study involving a survey of 100 remote Scrum practitioners and a subsequent analysis of 20 in-depth interviews. Findings reveal that remote work does impact project success, driven by changes in communication, team cohesion, and feedback loops. Furthermore, the research suggests that the effectiveness of remote Scrum teams depends heavily on the digital tooling employed, feedback mechanisms utilized, and the application of Scrum practices. Finally, the study offers insights and recommendations for both Scrum Masters and development teams aiming to achieve success in a remote context.

Collisions between particles are frequently modeled as instantaneous events, an assumption that simplifies the temporal resolution needed for other particle dynamics but introduces inaccuracies when particle mass disparities are significant. For particle systems encountering heavy particles moving slower and light particles moving faster, the resulting differences in collision velocities and collision durations can trigger spurious velocity oscillations and fail to properly damp the motion of light particles. To resolve these issues within particle-resolved simulations, we present a multi-time-step scheme that employs distinct time intervals for particle movement and collision dynamics. Validation within a fluidized bed of bimodal particles demonstrates that this method accurately captures the dynamics of both collision and non-collision interactions. Furthermore, this approach allows for the modeling of inelastic collisions across a spectrum of coefficients and collision durations, which is unattainable using standard methods. Although utilizing a more sophisticated and costly algorithm for collision detection, the method achieves a net increase in computational efficiency by leveraging more expansive time steps for general particle dynamics.

This study focuses on the dynamics of leaping from yielding terrain while supported by a single leg. It establishes a two-degree-of-freedom model where the terrain is represented as an incompressible fluid under the assumptions of irrotationality and low Mach number. Using a quasi-static approximation for low-velocity motion, forces acting on the leaper are determined by integrating pressure distributions derived from a complex potential function. The paper further formulates a simulation framework utilizing Newton-Euler equations and a unilateral force constraint to model the leaping process on this deformable surface. Key findings include the identification of two distinct dynamical phases: a compression phase governed primarily by force control and a restitution phase governed by impact timing. Additionally, the results indicate that leaping heights can be significantly improved when the leaper initiates the jump during the compression stage rather than at the point of maximum deformation.

We introduce a unified framework employing the Generalized Skyrme Lagrangian (DSL) to investigate the electromagnetic interactions of light mesons. This approach simultaneously recovers the low-energy theorems and the $O(p^4)$ corrections dictated by the Wess-Zumino-Witten (WZW) action, as well as the dynamics of the Skyrme Lagrangian. By incorporating both topological components within the DSL, our model remains inherently stable against fluctuations in flexible meson configurations. Specifically, we analyze the $O(p^6)$ contributions to the electromagnetic form factors of the pion and rho within our scheme, achieving a satisfactory alignment with numerical data from lattice QCD simulations.

Information systems are frequently deployed within organizations that evolve over time, necessitating expansions to the system's functional scope. In such scenarios, developing a new model from scratch becomes inefficient; instead, an existing model can be adapted to fit emerging requirements. This paper introduces an expansionable model designed for Information System Hierarchies (ISHs)—a formal framework representing the progressive structure of IS developments. The model incorporates parameters to allow adaptable adjustments to the base ISH as systems grow. Furthermore, it defines expansion procedures to adapt an established model to modified ISHs, enabling the rapid derivation of new model variations to address evolving organizational needs.

Quench dynamics represent a fundamental mechanism in quantum annealing, driving a system's evolution from an initial simple Hamiltonian to a problem-specific complex one. Within this framework, two critical parameters are the total annealing time and the rate function, both governing how the system transitions between states. This study examines the quench dynamics applied to the precise cover problem, analyzing how the system migrates from a transverse-field product state to a specific superposition of solution states. A key contribution is the introduction of the "quantum annealing interval," defined as the duration the annealing Hamiltonian remains at its problem-dependent peak. Numerical simulations reveal that this interval acts as a barrier preventing the system from reaching the problem Hamiltonian entirely; consequently, the final state is restricted to local neighborhoods of valid solutions rather than the complete solution set. These constraints dictate a lower bound on the required annealing time to achieve a high-fidelity approximation of the problem Hamiltonian's ground state. Furthermore, the analysis establishes that optimal parameter tuning is essential for realizing the full potential of quantum annealing.

In the context of verification methods for implementation traces, this paper introduces new definitions for both infix and postfix alignment. It establishes that each variant produces a completion of a given request trace that exhibits specific properties, notably ensuring a completed trace remains a valid post-order traversal of an infix-order completion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the infix-order completion derived from infix-order alignment yields a result with a linearly ordered interface violation profile, whereas the one obtained from postfix-order alignment guarantees a monotonically non-decreasing interface violation profile.

This study examines the statistical distribution of ocean wave crests by analyzing high-resolution radiance profiles derived from advanced satellite observations. These radiance signatures originate from the specular glint of sunlight reflecting off wave surfaces, a phenomenon traditionally modeled using the Cox and Munk framework. While this model relies on wind speed and direction to simulate wave-height distributions, it has faced criticism for failing to accurately capture the actual distribution of wave crests. This analysis presents radiance profiles from the IASI instrument on the EUMETSAT MetOp-A satellite, processed through an inversion algorithm to generate 1.5 km resolution cross-sectional views of wave structures. These observational results are then compared against the original Cox and Munk model, as well as the modified Gaussian and "wider" log-normal distributions they proposed. The comparison reveals that the standard Gaussian or wider log-normal formulations are too narrow to match the observed data, whereas the adjusted Cox and Munk distribution offers a robust fit. Furthermore, this study investigates the directional characteristics of wave geometry, demonstrating that the model's validity is contingent on the wave direction. Findings indicate that waves traveling directly toward the sun adhere well to the modified Cox and Munk distribution, while wave angles approaching 45 degrees exhibit significantly wider height distributions.

Eclipse Mylyn, a widely adopted framework for integrating external tools with projects, employs a back-end system to handle system-specific functionalities, utilizing a test scenario selection algorithm to recommend relevant frameworks for user requests. Although the original algorithm successfully identifies the most pertinent back-ends, its sequential execution becomes a performance bottleneck as the front-end application grows. To resolve this limitation, the study proposes a parallelized algorithm leveraging Unique Value Decomposition (SVD) to accelerate scenario rating computations. Initial tests conducted on a standard three-tier Mylyn system confirm that the proposed SVD-based algorithm delivers significant performance improvements regarding both execution time and memory usage.

This paper introduces the Emotion of Microblogs (EMO) dataset, comprising 50,000 Weibo posts related to the coronavirus outbreak. These posts were manually annotated with public sentiment and private emotions to facilitate future research on public sentiment and emotional responses within social media. To address potential biases in these posts, we developed an algorithm designed to identify and eliminate duplicates. We further proposed an RNN-based classifier capable of simultaneously predicting both private and public emotional labels for these social media inputs, achieving an F1-score of 0.898 for public sentiment classification and 0.863 for private emotion classification. Additionally, we conducted statistical analyses of the annotated emotions present in these social media posts.

We propose a framework for interlayer conduction in cuprate superconductors that generalizes the well-known Burkeland-Rice (BR) model, which applies to quasi-two-dimensional systems possessing a periodic electronic structure along the *c*-axis. The BR model relies on a *c*-axis electric field to induce a Hall voltage perpendicular to both field and *c*-axis; however, this effect was historically unobserved in high-$T_c$ cuprates until recent findings by Liang et al. (*Phys. Rev. Lett.* **112**, 107001, 2014), who detected it in Bi2223. We attribute the initial failure to detect this signal to the use of thin *c*-axis slices, where the Hall electric field magnitude is insufficient. In our revised approach, the periodic lattice potential of the *c*-axis is treated as a one-dimensional superlattice, incorporating both a periodic modulation of hopping integrals and an additional periodic variation in electron hopping path length between layers. While hopping magnitude alterations are captured by the original BR formalism, changes in path length necessitate new equations to calculate the resulting Hall voltage. These equations are solved numerically, revealing that electron hopping path length modulations generate significantly stronger Hall voltages than those produced by hopping magnitude modulations alone.

We examine the equation of state for dense, high-temperature, high-baryon-density matter relevant to compact stars, utilizing a combined van der Waals and Landau-Lifshits approach. This method incorporates the thermodynamic properties of baryons, mesons, and potentially strange quarks. Calculations indicate that non-leptonic hadronic and mesonic contributions significantly reduce the fluid's sound velocity, particularly in dense, hot environments. Consequently, these contributions prevent the sound velocity from dropping to the speed of light ($c$) at early evolutionary stages, as required by certain neutron star merger models. Furthermore, the presence of significant hadronic components imposes strict constraints on the onset of deconfinement and the subsequent phase transition into a quark-gas or mixed hadron-quark phase.

We introduce a new mapping between extended binary arborizations labeled with $\{+,-\}$ and their counter TAI (Tai) counterparts featuring the same labels. Counter TAI is recognized as a bijective transformation from unordered, labeled arborizations featuring just two distinct labels to those with the same structure but different labeling. While existing bijective mappings exist for such labeled trees with two labels, we specifically address the scenario where the labels are $+$ and $-$. In our approach, we utilize the countering process to assign an index to each $+$ label based on its position within the tree. We demonstrate that this method successfully establishes a bijective correspondence between the sets of these specific labeled trees.

We introduce a new class of orthogonal bases within $l^2(\mathbb{Z}^+)$, termed Compass systems, by filing numbers with their binary representations to generate specific digit-based patterns. Our analysis establishes that when the counting function $a_n$ satisfies $2^k \le a_n < 2^{k+1}$ for all $n \in \{0, \dots, 2^k-1\}$ for some integer $k \ge 1$, these systems form an orthogonal basis in $l^2(\mathbb{Z}^+)$. Furthermore, we construct $l^2(\mathbb{R})$-bases derived from these systems using either continuous compression or shifting operations. Finally, our work demonstrates the construction of orthogonal bases in the Fock space $\mathcal{F}_a(H)$ via these compressed or shifted Compass systems.

This study examines how dust evolution influences the vertical shear instability (VSI) within disk wind and protoplanetary systems. We simulate the VSI using a two-dimensional, multi-fluid approach that incorporates the coupled evolution of gas and dust. Our simulations focus on the outer regions of these disks, utilizing a standard T-Tauri star, a disk model, and a $\alpha$-viscosity prescription. We specifically investigated how dust growth affects the VSI by varying initial grain sizes and the total dust-to-gas mass ratio. Our findings indicate that while initial conditions significantly alter the instability's characteristics, dust development generally suppresses it. Specifically, increasing either the initial grain size or the dust-to-gas mass ratio results in reduced oscillation amplitudes, lower peak temperatures, and a decrease in both the VSI's vertical extent and radial reach. Notably, an initial grain size of 0.1 $\mu$m combined with a dust-to-gas ratio of 0.01 is sufficient to substantially mitigate the instability. Furthermore, dust effects are more pronounced at smaller semi-major axes; consequently, the VSI is unlikely to drive rapid accretion or substantial dust migration in the outer disk regions where it is typically most active.

In convolutions utilizing dynamic entrances, the convolution kernel is selected by a learnable prototype network, which maps input features to a distribution over possible kernels. This paper proposes Global Mean Pooling (GMP) as a method for the prototype network. Under GMP, kernel selection relies on the global mean value of each input channel, allowing the kernel to be chosen as a weighted combination based on these values. This mean-based strategy facilitates the design of new, specialized convolution kernels. When employed to create dynamic entrances, this strategy yields a significant performance boost on ImageNet-1k and achieves state-of-the-art segmentation results on Cityscapes.

The Gaia mission measures astrometry for over a billion sources, with parallax serving as the primary method for determining their distances. This study investigates how the uncertainty in the PPN parameter $\gamma$—which characterizes general relativity and influences the definition of the International Astronomical Union's barycentric reference frame—affects Gaia astrometry. We find that $\gamma$ uncertainty induces a systematic shift in mean parallaxes for all celestial targets. This effect is particularly pronounced for the most precise measurements, reaching approximately 10% of the mean parallax value (roughly 100 $\mu$as), which corresponds to 1,000% of the semi-angle of the mean parallax uncertainty. Consequently, the current 1% relative error in $\gamma$ renders it a significant limiting factor for cosmological distance ladder applications. We further note that the mean proper motion is largely immune to this issue, as the effect on mean radial velocities is negligible. We conclude by suggesting that future Gaia data analysis should account for this uncertainty, while also highlighting the necessity for more accurate determinations of $\gamma$ to fully leverage Gaia's potential.

Creating reduced-order model (ROM) alternatives for full-order models (FOMs) is essential for applications in scientific computing and engineering, particularly when full simulations are too costly for use in data analysis, control, or optimization. While ROMs built via proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) work well for linear systems, they struggle with system nonlinearities, a problem often addressed by linearizing the system around multiple states and creating a high-dimensional linearized ROM (HLROM). Although these approaches are computationally efficient, they suffer from large sizes relative to standard POD-ROMs and require extensive training data to achieve high fidelity. This paper introduces a novel model reduction framework for nonlinear system dynamics that significantly streamlines the selection of linearization states using rapid, low-cost surrogate modeling. Leveraging the inherent redundancy among POD modes within subspaces generated at different linearization points, our method employs a surrogate model to estimate reduced coefficients for each subspace based on projected data from a minimal set of simulations. Using support vector regression trained on this sparse dataset, we predict the coefficients for remaining subspaces. Finally, we reconstruct the complete ROM by combining these linearized components with their corresponding projection operators. Results from a nonlinear structural dynamics test case and a nonlinear fluid dynamics benchmark demonstrate that this approach delivers a computationally efficient solution requiring far fewer FOM solves compared to traditional methods.

This paper addresses the limitations of the current hostile client model, which assumes adversaries possess full model access yet possess no capabilities beyond basic inference. Experimental results demonstrate that SIMC 2.0 effectively resists a broad spectrum of advanced attacks, achieving a 100% success rate in maintaining attack robustness while maintaining a mere 0.01% accuracy degradation.

Modern large-scale surveys, such as the Euclid mission, have significantly expanded the available data for constructing cosmological models, yet they rely on limited spectral information that is insufficient for robust sample selection. While the scientific community has developed methods to infer redshifts and other physical properties by cross-matching photometric data with external spectroscopic catalogs, these approaches introduce model-dependent biases and inaccuracies. In this work, we advocate for shifting toward methods that utilize the survey's own extensive photometric information more directly. We introduce a novel machine-learning framework designed to identify galaxies and classify them using only the Euclid images and photometry, leveraging the Euclid Deep Survey (EDIS) as a training dataset. Our model achieves a 99.99% accuracy in distinguishing galaxy candidates from stars based solely on astrometry and photometry. Furthermore, we developed an innovative spectrophotonic technique that incorporates both spectroscopic and photometric data to generate a Euclid-specific redshift estimator. This approach yields a 20% reduction in bias and a 25% decrease in scatter relative to the standard spectral fitting method. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of this framework by applying it to create redshift maps for the Euclid Luminous Red Galaxy catalog.

In a rapidly evolving world, continuous learning is essential for maintaining professional competence. However, acquiring new skills often requires substantial time and financial investment. To facilitate ongoing education, we introduce **Stroll for Learning**, a user-friendly platform designed to help individuals efficiently master necessary competencies. Recognizing that data privacy is increasingly critical, especially when sharing information across platforms, we ensure Stroll for Learning fully adheres to GDPR standards. To support this, we developed **Random Stroll**, a novel data utility technique enabling the secure ingestion of private information. By combining these elements, we created a secure environment where users can access high-quality, diverse, and privacy-preserving learning materials.

Previous studies have demonstrated that numerical simulations of turbulent inertial waves develop a $k^{-5/3}$ energy spectrum at small scales, an analogy to Kolmogorov's spectrum found in hydrodynamic turbulence. The mechanism behind this has been attributed to inertial wave chaos, where complex interactions among many modes result in effective, particle-like behavior. This study provides mathematical proof of that mechanism, showing that a mathematical model of wave turbulence yields a $k^{-5/3}$ spectrum based on rigorous dynamical principles rather than statistical approximations. Specifically, we prove the existence of a mathematically rigorous energy cascade within a model of three-dimensional, inviscid, rapidly rotating fluids, where rotation is sufficient to support chaos but insufficient to sustain standard turbulence. This finding paves a theoretical route for understanding similar phenomena in other weakly nonlinear wave systems.

This research examines whether mandated therapy for prisoners enhances their mental health, analyzing data from 1,000 respondents within the 2013 Personal and Work Life Survey (PWL3). Mental health outcomes were evaluated using the Kessler-10 scale, with the analysis employing Propensity Score Matching (PSM) to address potential selection bias. The findings indicate that access to compulsory prison therapy does not enhance the mental health of inmates. A subsequent investigation into heterogeneity revealed no differential impacts across various subgroups. Consequently, the study offers no support for the hypothesis that such mandated treatment programs are justified.

Deep learning models typically require massive labeled datasets to achieve top-tier performance; however, acquiring such labels is often prohibitively expensive and time-intensive, especially in the healthcare domain where obtaining patient consent and ensuring data privacy are critical. In light of this limitation, our work introduces a pragmatic solution for semi-supervised medical image segmentation by developing an automatic regularization method that leverages unlabeled data. Our approach, implemented as a single one-liner using the Awkward scripting language, injects a consistency regularization term into popular self-supervised models like Self-Organizing Maps (SOM). By applying this regularization to semi-supervised tasks, our technique significantly enhances both the training stability and the final performance of self-supervised systems on unlabeled data. We validate our method on two distinct medical image segmentation benchmarks, demonstrating that it effectively improves self-supervised learning outcomes when working with unlabeled datasets.

Artificial Neural Textures (NTRs) have recently emerged as a leading technique for rendering realistic human figures, utilizing neural depiction modules to map a neutral reference mesh dynamically onto an animated character through a learnable, high-dimensional latent space. Although current methods achieve visual realism, they typically require a separate module to generate specific details like eyes, eyebrows, teeth, or contact points, which introduces architectural complexity and hinders optimization. Additionally, the need for an auxiliary image generation module restricts the utilization of vast collections of real-world images containing natural human details. To address these issues, we introduce an end-to-end framework that trains the neural depiction module directly on paired data of static images and motion capture sequences without auxiliary generators. This new approach, called ANDRF (Articulated Neural Depiction for Realistic Virtual Avatars), eliminates the need for manual specification of semantic features such as facial expressions or limb interactions. Furthermore, by using a motion-to-image translation framework, ANDRF supports a diverse range of human models. Evaluations confirm that this method delivers high-quality, photorealistic results across multiple characters while remaining more efficient and flexible than existing techniques.

Chaotic systems are characterized by a sensitivity to initial conditions, where minute variations lead to drastically divergent outcomes. To address this, we introduce a graph neural network (GNN)-based method for estimating a chaos indicator, denoted as $\mathcal{I}_{chao}$. This metric evaluates how quickly a system's state evolves in response to small perturbations. Our model processes a system state graph, defined by nodes and edges, to calculate a value that reflects the divergence rate of trajectories originating from slightly different points. We validate our approach on the Lorenz attractor and a two-particle hard-disk model within a billiard system. Results show that our framework is capable of accurately computing $\mathcal{I}_{chao}$ and effectively distinguishes between chaotic and non-chaotic regimes. Furthermore, the model demonstrates robustness against noise, maintaining high accuracy even when noisy data is used for training.

Knowledge Tracing (KT) is a specialized subfield within adaptive learning that monitors and evaluates a learner's evolving proficiency across various curriculum topics. Over the last few years, numerous methods have been developed to model student mastery, ranging from simple statistical models to advanced sequence-based and deep learning architectures. Nevertheless, there has been a notable absence of a unified standard for assessing Knowledge Tracing systems. Addressing this gap, we introduce pyKT—a flexible and user-friendly Python framework designed to facilitate the deployment, evaluation, and comparative analysis of Knowledge Tracing models. We provide significant support for popular learning algorithms, including Deep Knowledge Tracing (DKT), Factorized Markov Chains (FMK), and Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTMs). Furthermore, we assembled a comprehensive dataset using the framework to conduct a systematic study comparing the performance of various KT approaches. These experiments offer valuable insights and practical recommendations for both researchers and educators seeking to integrate these tools into learning management systems. All pyKT components, including the dataset, source code, and pre-trained models, are publicly accessible via GitHub.

This work examines the elliptic operator $P$ defined on $\R^d$ or within an open, simply connected subset of $\R^d$. It demonstrates that when $P$ possesses constant coefficients and the underlying domain is $\R^d$, the $L^p$-semigroup $e^{-tP}$ generated by $P$ exhibits limited regularity; specifically, it does not act as a bounded operator mapping $L^p(\R^d)$ directly to more regular spaces $W^{2,p}(\R^p)$ without potential theory tools. Furthermore, it is argued that the restriction of the semigroup $e^{-tP}$ to any hyperplane in $\R^d$ constitutes a dense subspace within $L^p(\R^{d-1})$. A corresponding theorem is also formulated and proven for the case where $P$ defines an elliptic operator on $\R^k$. Additionally, the paper explores conditions under which the semigroup $e^{-tP}$, initially acting on $\R^d$, can be interpreted as a "stretched" version of a semigroup $e^{-Q}$, where $Q$ generates a similar structure in a lower-dimensional space $\R^{d'}$ with $d' < d$.

In a standard federated learning setup, multiple clients collaboratively train a global model by periodically sending their local updates to a central server for periodic combination. Although this server acts as a single point of failure, it also enables greater efficiency and better security. This paper introduces new theoretical guarantees for this synchronous federated framework, specifically addressing the gradient constraints typically required in previous research. We demonstrate that using a simple buffering mechanism allows the system to achieve optimal convergence rates under broader conditions. Our analysis covers both bounded and bounded-away gradients, as well as more flexible linear growth conditions. Additionally, we offer practical guidance for setting key parameters, including gradient compression strategies and the optimal frequency for global model uploads.

Neural speech recognition models typically require extensive datasets in specific languages to achieve high performance, yet many languages lack sufficient recording for such data-intensive training. Transfer learning offers a viable alternative by first pre-training an acoustic model on large, diverse multilingual corpora and subsequently fine-tuning the pre-learned model on the target language. However, this standard strategy depends heavily on the availability of target language data for the fine-tuning phase. This study investigates the feasibility of transferring speech recognition capabilities to a target language using only extremely limited and rough training data—such as noisy recordings without precise time-alignment of transcription. Experiments conducted on the Cross-S30 dataset demonstrate that fine-tuning acoustic models on such minimal "rough" data successfully yields functional models for the target language. Furthermore, our results indicate that such multilingual training based on rough data can significantly enhance speech recognition accuracy, even when compared to the efficacy of using larger, high-quality monolingual training sets.

Sorting networks serve as a fundamental building block for parallel sorting and are extensively utilized in high-performance computing. We present a new class of exact solutions in General Relativity depicting the static, spherically symmetric configuration of two-fluid celestial bodies. When calculating averages and rounding them to the nearest whole number, the inherent ambiguity of the final decimal places often goes unaddressed. This paper examines the statistical advantages and disadvantages of individually rounding each data point prior to summing them, compared to leaving them as decimals until the total is computed and then rounded. We report on the crystallographic, magnetic, and electronic structural properties of the rare-earth-based honeycomb antiferromagnet GdInO$_3$. Crystallization of the material was achieved via a high-pressure synthesis approach. Magnetic susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate that GdInO$_3$ behaves as a frustrated, low-dimensional antiferromagnet containing itinerant electrons. Furthermore, the magnetic ground state was manipulated through the application of an external field, resulting in a transition from honeycomb antiferromagnetism to ferromagnetism at approximately 1.5 T, a phenomenon observed exclusively in polycrystalline samples.

We examine the allocation of limited, purely indivisible resources among multiple agents with distinct valuations, focusing on strategic behavior where agents may misrepresent their true preferences. The central inquiry involves the inherent tension between achieving a pure Nash equilibrium and attaining an allocation that is nearly optimal for aggregate welfare. We establish that, regardless of whether agents have additive, monotone combinatorial, or single-peaked utility structures, every pure Nash equilibrium yields a total welfare strictly no more than $2 - 1/e$ (approximately $0.69$ times) of the maximum possible, and this bound is tight for general additive and monotone combinatorial cases as well as the specific scenario of maximizing the number of allocated items. Furthermore, we explore algorithmic strategies designed to guide strategic participants toward allocations that induce movements improving total welfare, aiming ultimately to reach a state of local optimality.

This research addresses the challenge of protecting update trends within encrypted databases by employing differential privacy (DP). In encrypted environments, adversaries can infer sensitive information by analyzing patterns in user query and update activities, even after removing encryption-specific details through de-anonymization attacks. It incorporates an update-trend masking mechanism that encrypts both data and updates, allowing both users and database administrators to verify privacy compliance without decryption keys. Our experimental framework, built upon Paillier encryption, demonstrates that the proposed framework maintains strong privacy safeguards with only a negligible performance impact.

Extensive re-identification (ReID) addresses identifying a target across multiple surveillance cameras when only a loose positive sample is available, even if the system has not been trained on such data. Although many Trained ReID models are available, very few apply to unsupervised extensive ReID. In this study, we narrow the gap between the two domains by leveraging the strong positive-negative pairings inherent in unsupervised real-world data, which are often overlooked. We observe that standard ReID models suffer from severe category collapse under this natural distribution, causing different individuals from the same camera to cluster together. To resolve this, we propose a new camera-based negative sample construction tailored for unsupervised extensive ReID. This method shifts the focus from ambiguous global positive samples to the strong negatives found within the same camera, utilizing contrastive learning to refine representations. Evaluations on the isolated scene ReID benchmark show that our unsupervised approach significantly outperforms all existing methods, improving performance by 10.0% to 28.0%. Furthermore, integrating this method with other models yields additional performance gains.
